newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong confirms no trade changes under China.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong confirms no trade changes under China.

text.p: There will be no merger of trade statistics, textile quotas or a change in the "Made in Hong Kong" label following the territory's return to China, a leading Hong Kong trade official said on Friday.

"Hong Kong will continue to be a full and separate member of the (World Trade Organisation), using the name 'Hong Kong, China', and we will continue to implement faithfully our obligations under the WTO Agreement on Textiles and Clothing," said assistant director of trade, Patrick Nip.
Hong Kong became a Special Administrative Region within China on July 1, ending 156 years of British colonial rule.

Nip stressed that under the "one country, two systems" policy guiding the sovereignty transition, Hong Kong will remain a separate customs territory within China and that the regime governing the textiles and clothing trade would remain unchanged.
He also repeated Hong Kong's commitment to uphold its multilateral and bilateral obligations and said it would remain fully committed to vigilance against any attempt to abuse the origin rules.

"We will continue with our initiatives to enhance our textiles control system. We will continue to work with our trading partners to enhance both sides' effectiveness in the common objective of tackling illegal transshipment," he said.

"At the same time, we will seek to ensure that any action taken by our trading partners should not be discriminatory in nature, should not target Hong Kong and should not affect adversely legitimate traders."
In June last year, the United States imposed a series of additional import measures targeting certain garments imported from Hong Kong, but modified the measures this year.

From July 1 this year, the United States set a new term bond requirement for companies importing textiles and apparel products, regardless of the source of the imports, set at two percent of the value of world-wide imports for the previous calendar year.
Lower and upper ceilings were set at US$50,000 and $30 million respectively.
"We note that this is an improvement over the June 1996 arrangements under which Hong Kong was singled out for a single entry bond requirement," Nip said.

"However, we need to continue to keep a close watch on the implementation of the new term bond requirement to ensure that in practice there will be no discriminatory treatment against Hong Kong's import."
Hong Kong would continue to fight any discriminatory treatment against Hong Kong importers, he added.

"We will pursue further with the US Customs on the early removal of any discriminatory treatment against Hong Kong, in particular the importer's certification and additional documentation requirement for entries from 'suspect manufacturers'," he said.
